title: They Didn't Believe She Wrote Her Own Poems.

beats.text: They didn't believe she wrote her own poems.

overlays.hook: They didn't believe *she wrote her own poems.*

beats.text: Around 1761, a girl of about seven was kidnapped from West Africa and shipped to Boston on a slave ship, the Phillis.

visual.caption: The town of Boston, engraving by Paul Revere, 1770

beats.text: John Wheatley bought her for his wife. They named her after the ship.
Within a few years she was reading Greek and Latin. At about fourteen, she published her first poem.
But when she had a book of poems, people wanted proof. Could an enslaved African girl really write them?
So eighteen powerful Boston men, the governor and John Hancock among them, signed a statement: she wrote them.

visual.title: 18 signatures
visual.sub: "written by Phillis, a young Negro girl"

beats.text: In 1773, her book was printed in London: the first book of poems by an African American.

visual.caption: Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, London, 1773

beats.text: Soon after, she was freed. In 1775 she sent a poem to George Washington. He wrote back.
She married, lost her children, and fell into poverty. She died in 1784, about thirty-one.

visual.caption: Her book of poems, 1773, Old South Meeting House, Boston

beats.text: They didn't believe she wrote her own poems. She did.

facts.claim: Born c. 1753 in West Africa (Senegal/Gambia region); kidnapped and brought to Boston in 1761 on the slave ship Phillis.
Bought by John Wheatley for his wife Susanna; named after the ship.
Tutored by the Wheatley children; read the Bible, Greek and Latin classics; first poem published 1767 (about 14).
The book's attestation, signed by 18 Boston men incl. Governor Hutchinson, Lt-Governor Oliver and John Hancock (plus her master), says the poems were 'written by Phillis, a young Negro Girl'.
Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, London, 1 Sept 1773; first African American to publish a book of poetry.
Freed by late 1773; poem to Washington 26 Oct 1775; Washington invited her to his headquarters.
Married John Peters 1778; children died; died 5 Dec 1784 at about 31.

notUsed: Whether an oral 'examination' by the 18 men actually took place (the attestation says she 'has been examined by some of the best Judges'; scholars debate the scene)
Whether she actually visited Washington (NWHM: likely never accepted)
Exact age at capture; '16 months' to learn English
'In poverty': her husband jailed for debt, she worked as a scullery maid (Wikipedia only) - the reel says 'fell into poverty', post gives detail
